claims.text: Adding low-density elements such as Al or Ti reduces the overall density of the modified HEA relative to the baseline.
Low-density alloying additions promote controlled elemental partitioning during solidification.
Solidification-induced partitioning produces coherent nanoscale precipitates.
Coherent nanoscale precipitates strengthen the matrix by impeding dislocation motion.
The precipitates serve as nucleation sites or templates for a stable, protective oxide film at elevated temperatures.
Precipitation strengthening and precipitate-mediated passivation jointly enable high strength, corrosion resistance, and oxidation resistance despite reduced density.
The proposed initial alloy can have a single-phase or dual-phase microstructure containing fine, coherent precipitates.
The coherent precipitates and associated oxide films are evenly distributed within a fine-grained matrix.
The controlled comparison should hold processing and environmental conditions constant while varying the targeted lightweight-element additions.
The modified alloy should retain yield and ultimate strength comparable to or greater than the baseline.
The modified alloy should have better corrosion resistance than the baseline.
The modified alloy should have better high-temperature oxidation resistance than the baseline.
The baseline alloy has higher density than the modified alloy.
The baseline alloy relies on conventional solid-solution strengthening.
Temperatures beyond the precipitate stability limit will coarsen or dissolve the coherent precipitates.
Aggressive chemical media can disrupt the protective oxide layer.
Disrupting the precipitate network or protective oxide will reduce the combined benefits to the level of, or below, the baseline.
Related HEA observations qualitatively support a joint role for nanoscale precipitation in strengthening and passivation.
If intentional precipitate coarsening or dissolution does not degrade performance, the proposed precipitate-mediated mechanism is falsified.

contradictions.description: The prediction permits mechanical strength merely comparable to the baseline, whereas the falsification rule requires a significant improvement in mechanical strength as well as corrosion/oxidation resistance. A result allowed by the prediction could therefore be labeled falsifying.

The initial state permits a single-phase alloy while the required mediator is a population of coherent precipitates, which ordinarily constitutes an additional phase; the intended meaning may instead be a single-phase matrix containing a precipitate phase.
